doc.title: Keter Betts interviewed by Monk Rowe, Sarasota, Florida, April 11, 1996

title: Joining Earl Bostic's rhythm and blues band
summary: He joined Bostic in 1949 to see the country, recommended Jimmy Cobb, played a date with Dinah Washington and left for her band in late 1951.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money

blocks.x: Now getting with Earl Bostic, was he doing straight ahead jazz?
He was doing rhythm & blues, so you got a new —

I think the reason that I did that was the fact that I was going to get a chance to travel and see the country. You know, after studying geography, which you don’t have in the schools now anymore, but after studying geography I said well I’ll get a chance to see the country, it’ll be a new experience, and it was. And at that time there was hardly no, you know like no freeways, there was none. In fact the only thing that you had was save for like the Merrick Parkway, there were a few of those around the country. The Pennsylvania Turnpike was like from 20 miles outside of Harrisburg to about 19 miles outside of Pittsburgh. That was it. And the rest of it, you went out to California it was 66, you know, the whole bit. But I got to see the country. And you’d be surprised at — I went in in April of ‘49 and in 1950 I got Jimmy Cobb with Bostic because Bostic needed a drummer and I recommended Jimmy Cobb. And we had to do a one-nighter with Dinah Washington in I think it was early ‘51. And she was just carrying a piano player with her. And so we had to do a set with her, a couple of sets with her, and she said, “listen, if you guys ever leave Bostic, you’ve got a job with me.” And so we left at the end of ‘51 and went with Dinah. And the young piano player was Wynton Kelly. So here were are now, when I joined Bostic’s band, I’m 19 years old, I’m the youngest guy in the band — no I’m 20 years old and the youngest guy in the band. And I went with Dinah a few years later, and I’m the oldest guy in the band and I’m 23.
